name: Baking soda toothpaste
summary: Sodium bicarbonate toothpaste sold for plaque, stain and odour control; the research is mostly on gum health, not whitening.
lead: Baking soda toothpaste is a dentifrice that contains sodium bicarbonate, usually alongside fluoride, marketed for plaque removal, stain removal, and neutralising acid and odour. Sodium bicarbonate is classed as a mild abrasive and appears in many "natural" toothpaste formulations.

name: Dentist deep cleaning (scaling and root planing)
summary: A dentist-performed non-surgical cleaning below the gumline that is the standard first treatment for periodontitis.
lead: Scaling and root planing, often called deep cleaning, is a non-surgical dental procedure that removes plaque and calculus from tooth surfaces above and below the gumline and smooths the exposed root surfaces. It is the usual first step in treating periodontitis, the gum disease that causes gum pockets, bone loss and eventual tooth loss.

name: Periodontal treatment
summary: The umbrella of professional and home care for gum disease, from deep cleaning to surgery and lifelong maintenance.
lead: Periodontal treatment is the set of professional and home-care measures used to manage periodontal (gum) disease, which ranges from gingivitis to periodontitis with bone loss and tooth loss. Options include home plaque control, professional root-surface instrumentation, surgery for advanced cases, local or systemic antibiotics, lifestyle changes and ongoing maintenance.

name: Gum grafting
summary: Surgery that moves palate or donor tissue onto receding gums to cover roots; the best-known recession fix, with a painful donor site.
lead: Gum grafting is a periodontal plastic surgery in which gum tissue, usually taken from the palate or from a donor source, is placed at a site with gum recession or too little keratinised tissue. It is used to cover exposed roots and to thicken or widen the gum band, including cosmetically.

name: Pinhole surgical technique (gum recession)
summary: A keyhole gum-recession procedure that repositions tissue without a graft; small studies, limited long-term data.
lead: The pinhole surgical technique (PST) is a minimally invasive procedure for gum recession in which a small hole is made in the gum above the recession and specialised instruments are used through it to loosen the gum tissue and move it over the exposed root, without cutting or suturing a graft. It was described in a 2012 retrospective study of 43 consecutive patients with 121 recession sites, as an alternative to connective tissue grafts whose second surgical site causes morbidity.

name: Gum recession treatment
summary: The family of gum surgeries, mostly grafts, aimed at covering exposed roots; widely studied, outcomes vary by technique.
lead: Gum recession treatment refers to the procedures used to restore or cover gum that has pulled back from the teeth and exposed the roots. Recession is common: one meta-analysis cited in encyclopedic sources estimates that about 85 percent of people worldwide have it on at least one tooth, and a 2026 study puts the figure at roughly 81 percent. Periodontal disease is its most common cause.

name: Gingivectomy
summary: Surgical trimming of gum tissue, used for overgrowth, pockets and gummy smiles; well established in dentistry, with cosmetic outcomes depending on the cause of the gum display.
lead: Gingivectomy is a dental surgical procedure in which part of the gum tissue (gingiva) is removed. It is described as the oldest surgical approach in periodontal (gum disease) therapy and is usually performed either for appearance or to improve the outlook for a tooth . Common indications include suprabony periodontal pockets, enlarged gums (including drug-induced overgrowth), exposing more tooth for restorations, and reducing excessive gum display when smiling .

name: Tonsil stone removal
summary: Clearing tonsillar stones, a recognised contributor to bad breath, by rinsing, gentle manual removal or clinic procedures; evidence is mostly case reports and reviews.
lead: Tonsil stones, or tonsilloliths, are mineralised accumulations of debris in the crypts of the tonsils, most often the palatine tonsils. The unmineralised form is called chronic caseous tonsillitis. Wikipedia reports that stones contain bacterial biofilm and calcium salts, with aerobic bacteria on the surface and anaerobes at the core, and that up to about 10 percent of people may have them .

name: Tonsillectomy
summary: Surgical removal of the tonsils, discussed in looksmaxxing as a last-resort fix for severe tonsil stones and breath odour; guidelines support it for recurrent infection and sleep apnoea, not for stones.
lead: Tonsillectomy is the surgical removal of both palatine tonsils, usually under general anaesthesia. It is one of the most frequently performed operations in children, with the main indications being recurrent or chronic tonsillitis and obstructive sleep-disordered breathing .

name: Treating GERD for breath
summary: Managing acid reflux in the hope of improving bad breath; reflux is listed as a possible cause, though most researchers regard the stomach as an uncommon source.
lead: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is a chronic condition in which stomach contents repeatedly flow back into the oesophagus. Wikipedia reports a prevalence of roughly 10 to 20 percent in Western populations and lists symptoms including heartburn, regurgitation and an acidic taste . Bad breath is listed as a symptom, particularly in children .

name: Treating sinus infection for breath
summary: Treating sinusitis or post-nasal drip to improve breath odour; nasal sources are recognised in principle, but no breath-analysis trials have tested it.
lead: Sinusitis is inflammation of the nasal sinuses. Wikipedia lists bad breath among its symptoms, alongside facial pain, congestion and discoloured nasal discharge . In the halitosis literature, nasal odour is said to arise from sinus infection or foreign bodies, and halitosis is often described as a symptom of chronic rhinosinusitis, but the halitosis article states that gold-standard breath analysis has not been applied to test this .

name: H. pylori treatment
summary: Antibiotic eradication of Helicobacter pylori, well established for ulcers and gastric cancer prevention, but not shown by trials to improve bad breath.
lead: Helicobacter pylori is a spiral gram-negative bacterium that colonises the stomach. Wikipedia reports that around half to two-thirds of people worldwide are infected, most without symptoms, and that infection can cause chronic gastritis, peptic ulcers, gastric cancer and gastric MALT lymphoma . A 2023 Nature Reviews Disease Primers article describes it as usually acquired in childhood and persisting for life if untreated .

name: Carnivore diet breath
summary: Reports of bad breath on an all-meat diet; the idea is discussed, but no studies on carnivore breath specifically exist.
lead: Carnivore diet breath refers to the bad breath or unusual breath odour that some people report when eating only animal products, a pattern commonly called the carnivore or zero-carb diet. Within appearance-focused communities it is discussed as a social and grooming concern, alongside other low-carbohydrate or ketogenic eating patterns.

name: Cutting sugar for gums
summary: Eating less sugar to starve plaque bacteria; linked to cavities in research, but gum-specific trials are not found here.
lead: Cutting sugar for gums is the practice of reducing dietary sugar with the aim of lowering dental plaque and improving gum health. Proponents reason that plaque bacteria feed on sugars.

name: Vitamin C for gums
summary: Vitamin C reverses scurvy gum bleeding; dental trials of gum depigmentation are ongoing with little published.
lead: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is used or proposed for gum health, in the context of scurvy-related gum bleeding and, in recent dental trials, for gingival pigmentation treatments.

name: CoQ10 for gums
summary: A supplement studied as an add-on for gum inflammation; trials are registered but results are not found.
lead: Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10, ubiquinone) is a fat-soluble compound made by the body and sold as a supplement; it is studied as an adjunct therapy to reduce inflammation in periodontitis.

name: Vitamin D and K2 for teeth
summary: Folk claim that vitamins D and K2 rebuild teeth; bone research exists, dental trials do not.
lead: Vitamin D and vitamin K2 are discussed in folk claims that they help teeth remineralise. Vitamin K2 is a cofactor for osteocalcin, a protein involved in bone mineral formation.

name: Remineralising toothpaste
summary: Toothpastes with fluoride or mineral agents to repair early enamel damage; fluoride has the strongest evidence.
lead: Remineralising toothpastes are formulated to help redeposit calcium, phosphate or fluoride into demineralised enamel. Active ingredients include fluoride, nano-hydroxyapatite, amorphous calcium phosphate and bioactive glass.

name: Ozone therapy for gums
summary: Ozone applied to the mouth as a gum-disease treatment; ozone therapy broadly is unproven and the FDA says ozone has no demonstrated safe medical use.
lead: Ozone therapy for gums refers to the use of ozone (O3), applied as a gas, ozonated water or ozonated oil, in the mouth with the aim of treating gum disease and related dental problems. It is a dental application of the broader practice of ozone therapy, which introduces ozone into the body as an alternative medicine treatment.
claims: Ozone kills the bacteria behind gum disease without antibiotics

name: Pulling coconut oil for gums
summary: Swishing coconut oil as a gum remedy; ADA says no reliable studies support it, though the Canadian Dental Association does not expect harm.
lead: Oil pulling with coconut oil is the practice of swishing the oil in the mouth for a period and then spitting it out, like a mouthwash, in the hope of improving gum and oral health. It comes from Ayurvedic medicine, and sunflower, sesame, olive and herbal oils are also used.
claims: Swishing coconut oil heals gums and pulls out toxins

name: Hydrogen peroxide gum rinse
summary: Dilute peroxide swished as a gum antiseptic; some trial support for gingivitis but chlorhexidine is reported more effective.
lead: A hydrogen peroxide gum rinse is a diluted solution of hydrogen peroxide swished in the mouth as an antiseptic, used in the hope of reducing plaque and gum inflammation (gingivitis). Hydrogen peroxide is also found in many whitening products.
claims: A peroxide rinse calms inflamed gums

name: Gum massage / Stillman technique
summary: A gumline brushing/gum-massage method; little evidence was found in the sources reviewed.
lead: The Stillman technique is a toothbrushing method named for a dental researcher, associated with gentle gum stimulation or massage alongside cleaning at the gumline. Gum massage is discussed in online circles as a way to improve gum health.

name: Dry mouth management (Biotene)
summary: Saliva substitutes like Biotene give short-term dry-mouth relief; no topical therapy has strong evidence.
lead: Dry mouth management refers to products and habits used to relieve xerostomia, the sensation of a dry mouth, including saliva substitutes in the form of sprays, gels, rinses and lozenges. Biotene is a widely sold brand of such products.

name: Drinking water frequently
summary: Frequent sipping is commonly suggested for dry mouth; no trial evidence on odour was found.
lead: Drinking water frequently is a habit recommended in many dry-mouth and breath-care guides as a way to relieve a dry mouth and reduce mouth odour. Wikipedia lists water among saliva substitutes but cites no specific trial for it.

name: Quit smoking and vaping for breath
summary: Stopping tobacco and nicotine use to cut smoke odour and protect the gums; the gum-health link is well documented, appearance-specific trials are not.
lead: Quitting smoking and vaping for breath and oral appearance refers to the practice of stopping tobacco and nicotine use in order to reduce smoke odour on the breath and to protect the gums. It is discussed in looksmaxxing and grooming circles as a low-cost lifestyle change, alongside oral hygiene and dental care.

name: Retainer and mouthguard cleaning
summary: Routine cleaning of retainers and mouthguards to limit bacterial buildup and odour; plausible by analogy to dentures, but little direct study.
lead: Retainer and mouthguard cleaning refers to routine hygiene for removable oral appliances such as orthodontic retainers, sports mouthguards and night guards. In grooming-oriented communities it is mentioned as a way to avoid bacterial buildup and odour.

name: Laser iris depigmentation (Stroma laser)
summary: A laser procedure meant to lighten iris color; unapproved for cosmetic use per reference summaries, with glaucoma and cataract listed as risks and no trials found.
lead: Laser iris depigmentation is a procedure, promoted for cosmetic eye color change, in which a laser is directed at the iris to reduce its melanin pigment and lighten the eye, typically from brown toward a lighter shade. It is discussed in hardmaxxing communities as a way to change eye color without an implant.

name: NewColorIris cosmetic implants
summary: Silicone iris implants placed in healthy eyes to change color; published case series report glaucoma, corneal damage and vision loss, and the brand is described as no longer in use.
lead: NewColorIris is a brand of foldable silicone artificial iris implants that were surgically placed in the anterior chamber of healthy eyes to change eye color for cosmetic reasons. Artificial irises are marketed as an alternative to cosmetic contact lenses, and ophthalmologists have criticized implanting them in healthy eyes because of the risk of vision loss .

name: Hypnosis for eye color change
summary: The claim that hypnosis can change iris color; no studies have tested it and reference sources report no evidence hypnosis alters physical traits.
lead: Hypnosis for eye color change is a claim, found in fringe corners of appearance culture, that hypnosis, self-hypnosis or suggestion recordings can alter the color of a person's irises.
claims: Hypnosis or suggestion can change your eye color

name: Honey drops in eyes
summary: A folk claim that honey in the eyes lightens iris color; untested, and related lightening drops are advised against by ophthalmologists.
lead: Honey drops in eyes is a folk claim that putting diluted honey in the eyes can lighten the iris color. It appears in fringe eye-color discussions and is not an established cosmetic procedure.
claims: Honey drops will lighten your eyes
